extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists and writers interested in prose craft, serialization, and revision
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and aesthetic guidance for producing and revising long-form fiction (novels and serials), emphasising character delineation, prose style, pace of production, and ethical depiction. Drawn from an experienced novelist's reflection on craft, publication, and readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delineation of character as the highest merit
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest merit which a novel can have consists in perfect delineation of character, rather than in plot, or humour, or pathos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim foremost to portray characters fully and convincingly; prioritize character development over clever plotting or incidental humour/pathos. Character truth is the chief virtue of a novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid revealing the plot too soon
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot of _Orley Farm_ is probably the best I have ever made; but it has the fault of declaring itself, and thus coming to an end too early in the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep key plot resolutions or confessions from being announced prematurely; preserve tension and discovery rather than allowing the plot to 'unravel itself' in mid-tale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style matters as much as ideas: use popular, lucid language
rubrics_metrics.description: The vehicle which a writer uses for conveying his thoughts to the public should not be less important to him than the thoughts themselves. An author can hardly hope to be popular unless he can use popular language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft a lucid, accessible prose style suited to the intended readership. Attend to readability and commonly accepted rules of language so as not to 'disgust' readers by ignoring conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness and habitual ease in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: He must be correct, because without correctness he can be neither agreeable nor intelligible. Readers will expect him to obey those rules which they, consciously or unconsciously, have been taught to regard as binding on language; and unless he does obey them, he will disgust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn grammatical and stylistic 'rules' thoroughly and practice them until correct usage becomes natural and effortless in composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop fluent language through long prior training
rubrics_metrics.description: His language must come from him as music comes from the rapid touch of the great performer's fingers... All this must be learned and acquired,--not while he is writing that which shall please, but long before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest long-term rehearsal and reading to make fluent phrasing automatic; build habits so that language flows naturally during composition rather than being produced by conscious, halting choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't overthink words during first composition
rubrics_metrics.description: A man who thinks much of his words as he writes them will generally leave behind him work that smells of oil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obsessing over individual word choice in first drafts; trust trained fluency and reserve fine-tuning for revision to prevent stilted, laboured prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid composition can produce excellent work if concentrated
rubrics_metrics.description: When my work has been quicker done... the rapidity has been achieved by hot pressure, not in the conception, but in the telling of the story... I have trebled my usual average, and have done so in circumstances which have enabled me to give up all my thoughts for the time to the book I have been writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intensive, focused bursts of writing (temporary week(s) of isolation, more hours/days) can yield some of your best telling — provided conception and characterization have been worked out and you can concentrate fully on the task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise and guard against the errors of rapid writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid writing will no doubt give rise to inaccuracy... A singular nominative will be disgraced by a plural verb, because other pluralities have intervened and have tempted the ear into plural tendencies. Tautologies will occur...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect mechanical and stylistic slips (agreement errors, tautology, repetition) when writing fast; plan careful revision to catch these. Be aware of particular failure modes where the 'ear' is misled by intervening phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough revision practice: read several times (thrice manuscript, once in print)
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been my practice to read everything four times at least—thrice in manuscript and once in print. Very much of my work I have read twice in print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt multiple passes of revision and proofing (multiple manuscript readings and at least one printed proof) to reduce errors and polish style. Serial and book writers should not rely on a single read-through.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not send a book 'hot from the hand' to the printer
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer for the press is rarely called upon—a writer of books should never be called upon—to send his manuscript hot from his hand to the printer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow time between composition and submission for revision; treat book manuscripts differently from ephemeral press pieces and avoid immediate submission of fresh drafts for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use immersion and solitude to inhabit characters
rubrics_metrics.description: At such times I have been able to imbue myself thoroughly with the characters I have had in hand. I have wandered alone among the rocks and woods, crying at their grief, laughing at their absurdities, and thoroughly enjoying their joy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodically remove yourself from ordinary life (quiet spots, isolation) to live mentally in your characters' world; this focused immersion deepens character portrayal and emotional truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical responsibility in depicting wrongdoing (avoid glamorisation)
rubrics_metrics.description: It must ever be wrong to force a girl into a marriage with a man she does not love... I made known nothing which the purest girl could not but have learned, and ought not to have learned, elsewhere, and I certainly lent no attraction to the sin which I indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying immoral acts or temptations, handle them with moral clarity and purpose (e.g., to teach a lesson), avoiding sensational or titillating depiction that could be read as glamorising the wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain character continuity while allowing natural change over time
rubrics_metrics.description: I realised the necessity, not only of consistency,—which, had it been maintained by a hard exactitude, would have been untrue to nature,—but also of those changes which time always produces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When carrying characters across works or long arcs, preserve essential traits for recognisability but also show credible evolution: intensity, manner of expression, and behavior may grow or diminish with years and events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of overproduction and reader saturation with too-frequent releases
rubrics_metrics.description: I quite admit that I crowded my wares into the market too quickly,--because the reading world could not want such a quantity of matter from the hands of one author in so short a space of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider market and reader appetite when planning output: excessive frequency of publication can fatigue readers and reduce the perceived value of each work, even if produced competently.
